title: This Summer Was the Hottest Ever Recorded in the U.S.
summary: Did this summer feel extra hot to you? You're not imagining it. The summer of 2026 was the hottest ever recorded in the United States — at least in the last 132 years. Temperatures from June through August were 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.67 degrees Celsius) above average. That beats the old record from 2021. August alone was the hottest August ever measured. The report comes from NOAA, a government group that studies weather and oceans. But heat wasn't the only problem. This summer was also one of the driest on record. By September 1, more than half the country — 59.1% — was in a drought. That means the land was very dry because it hadn't rained enough. Puerto Rico got hit hard too: over 75% of it was in drought. Dry land means a higher risk of wildfires. In August, fires burned over 10,000 acres in eastern Washington and spread into Oregon. Fires also broke out in Nevada and Alaska. Wind gusts up to 111 miles per hour tore across South Dakota. A heatwave hit south Florida, and Hurricane Lala brought heavy rain and flooding to Hawaii. Scientists say climate change, caused mostly by human activities like driving cars and making things in factories, is making these extreme events worse. And they warn it will keep getting hotter unless we act.
why_it_matters: Hotter, drier summers can mean more wildfires, less water for farms, gardens and swimming pools, and more days when it's simply too hot to play outside safely.

background_read: NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) is a U.S. government group that keeps track of the weather, the oceans, and the climate.
Puerto Rico (an island in the Caribbean Sea that is part of the United States) was one of the places hit hardest by the dry weather.
When people burn fuels like gasoline and coal, gases such as carbon dioxide go into the air and hold in heat, which is why Earth is slowly getting warmer.
Article_Structure: WHO: NOAA, the government group that studies weather and oceans, and the scientists who study climate.
WHAT: A report showing that the summer of 2026 was the hottest ever recorded in the United States, and one of the driest.
WHERE: Across the whole country, with the worst fires and dry spells in Washington, Oregon, Nevada, Alaska, South Dakota, Florida, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico.
WHY: To show how hot and dry the country has become, and to warn that climate change is making extreme weather worse.

perspectives.description: They say the record-breaking heat fits a clear pattern and will keep getting worse unless people act.
They worry most about wildfires, running out of water, and crops drying up.
Some argue that new rules for cars and factories cost money and jobs, so they want changes to happen more slowly.
